description_block:
THE LEOPARD PRINT PAJAMAS FROM THE "GIRLS JUST WANT TO HAVE FUN" MUSIC VIDEO
1983
A Sheila Anne red trim leopard print pajama set, 34.

Belonging to her grandmother, the pajamas were worn in the music video for "Girls Just Want to Have Fun" from the She's So Unusual album (Portrait Records, 1983).

The video began playing on MTV in October 1983 and would go on to win "Best Female Video" at the inaugural 1984 MTV Video Music Awards. The lasting love for "Girls Just Want to Have Fun" transcends its dance-able pop sound. Lauper swapped pronouns and various lyrics to change the song from a male perspective about chasing women into a female anthem about autonomy, solidarity, and the importance of women and girls living their lives with freedom and joy.

She's So Unusual is Cyndi Lauper's debut solo studio album, released on 13 October 1983 by Portrait Records. Achieving four top five singles, Lauper became the first female singer to have four top five singles from one album the Hot 100. Singles include "Girls Just Want to Have Fun," "Time After Time," and "She Bop." Lauper earned several awards and accolades for the album, including "Best New Artist" at the 27th Annual Grammy Awards.

THE STORYBOARD FOR THE "TRUE COLORS" MUSIC VIDEO
1986
Nine pages of Xeroxed sketches stapled at the top left corner showing the transitions of scenes and the camera direction for the "True Colors" music video.
each sheet 11 x 17in

In her memoir, Cyndi described the making of the "True Colors" music video: "The video and song are about learning to love yourself and accept yourself...I wanted to show the spiritual connection between people and to convey an angelic vibe." 

"True Colors" reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on October 25, 1986, and peaked at number three in Australia and New Zealand, and number 12 on the UK Singles Chart. 

Forty years after the release of "True Colors", the song continues to resonate and inspire. In 2022, Cyndi performed the song at the ceremony where US President Joe Biden signed the Respect for Marriage Act into law, and in 2025, Billboard magazine ranked it number nine in their list of "The 100 Greatest LGBTQ+ Anthems of All Time".

1986
Comprising a Stella Fagin baby blue and white lace tie-front blouse, a hoop underskirt with strips of adhered newspaper and Paper Magazine pages, and a pair of painted heels, together with a "True Colors" life-size cardboard display figure. (4)
height of display 73 /12in; width 38in

In 1986, Laura Wills and Cyndi Lauper grabbed a vintage hoop underskirt, some newspapers and issues of Paper Magazine, and created one of the most iconic looks in music history. Paired with a baby blue vintage blouse, a pair of painted pumps, and blue lipstick, the look was styled by Laura Wills and photographed by Annie Leibovitz for the cover of True Colors. 

Laura Wills is the owner of the storied NYC vintage shop Screaming Mimi's, where Cyndi once was an employee. Laura and Cyndi's fashion inspired each other to push the limits of creativity.

Thirty-nine years later, in 2025 Chappell Roan wore a replica of the newspaper skirt to induct Cyndi Lauper into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

This look was worn on the album cover for True Colors, as well as the music video, and during the 1986/1987 True Colors World Tour. It is also featured in Lauper's True Colors World Tour 86-87 book. This lot is accompanied by a copy of the True Colors World Tour 86-87 book.

Cyndi Lauper wore these pieces, along with dozens of more accessories and a crystal-adorned chandelier headdress in the "True Colors" music video as well as a photoshoot for the April 1986 issue of Interview magazine. 

Following her success of True Colors, Lauper transcended her role as a pop star into a timeless female icon. Shot by Matthew Rolston and styled by Laura Wills of Screaming Mimi's, the portrait was an homage to a 1923 photograph of Hollywood silent movie star Mae Murray. 

Lauper loved the theatrical, Old Hollywood vision Rolston created so much that she requested to incorporate the ensemble in the "True Colors" music video, alongside her iconic newspaper skirt outfit.

This lot is accompanied by a copy of a behind-the-scenes photograph from the photoshoot.

description_block:
A 67TH ANNUAL TONY AWARD NOMINATION CERTIFICATE FOR KINKY BOOTS PRESENTED TO CYNDI LAUPER AND RELATED MATERIAL
2012-2013
Comprising an unframed Nomination Certificate for "Best Original Score (Music and/or Lyrics) Written for the Theater," a Class of 2013 Official Tony Award Yearbook, an award show program, a Tony Nominee ceramic mug, and an Outer Critics Circle Award for "Outstanding New Broadway Musical" presented to Cyndi Lauper and Harvey Fierstein. (5)
nomination certificate sheet 10 x 8in

Kinky Boots is a musical based on a 2005 British film by the same name written by Geoff Deane and Tim Firth and mostly inspired by true events. When Daryl Roth, a Tony Award-winning producer, saw the Kinky Boots film at the 2006 Sundance Film Festival, she felt that the story had the heart and soul to be a musical. In 2010, a creative team was assembled with Harvey Fierstein, and Cyndi Lauper as the writer for the musical numbers. 

The story follows Charlie Price, who inherits a shoe factory from his father in the north of England and forms a partnership with a cabaret performer and drag queen named Lola to produce a line of high-heeled boots to save the business. 

The original production of Kinky Boots premiered at the Bank of America Theatre in Chicago in October 2012, made its Broadway debut at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre in April 2013, and its West End debut in 2015. 

Kinky Boots was nominated for thirteen Tony nominations and won six, including "Best Musical, Best Actor" for Billy Porter and "Best Score" for Cyndi Lauper, her time as a Broadway songwriter. She is the first woman to win alone in that category. The musical's cast album premiered at number one on the Billboard Cast Albums chart and number fifty-one on the Billboard 200 chart. The show also won three Laurence Olivier Awards, including "Best New Musical."

Speaking to the success of the musical, Cyndi explained "It's a story about love and acceptance and friendship and overcoming obstacles and everyone can relate to that."

THE RAINBOW HEADDRESS AND NICOLE MILLER DRESS WORN AS GRAND MARSHAL AT THE WEST HOLLYWOOD PRIDE PARADE
2003
The headdress decorated with rhinestones, sequins, and multicolored feathers, with a Nicole Miller strapless multi-colored dress. (2)
height of headdress approximately 32in

Worn at the Gay Pride Parade in West Hollywood, California, 22 June 2003. Lauper was Grand Marshal at the Parade and headlined the Wells Fargo main stage. It was also Lauper's 50th birthday.

Always different from those around her, Cyndi felt a kinship to the marginalized. When she first left home, her neighbors Carl Eagleston and Gregory Natal (who also inspired her song "Boy Blue") took her under their wing and cared for her in a way no one else had. When Gregory passed away from HIV/AIDs in 1986, Cyndi took to heart her promise that he would be remembered. Her song "True Colors" became an anthem of the LGBTQIA+ movement, and in 2008, Cyndi Lauper, Lisa Barbaris, Jonny Podell, and Gregory Lewis founded True Colors United (formerly the True Colors Fund), to help combat the homelessness experienced by LGBTQ+ youth. The fund offers free training and resources and advocates in government and media to help ensure critical funding and services. In Cyndi's words, "We each have a personal responsibility to make sure LGBTQ+ youth are treated with dignity and respect."

sale_title: Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories, Part I
description_block:
A "TIME AFTER TIME" SHOE ASSEMBLAGE MOBILE MADE BY CYNDI LAUPER
2026
A pair of pumps hand-painted white, the interiors lined with glazed photographs of the sky and clouds, and the soles with handwritten lyrics to "Time After Time" and signed C Lauper, hung with twisted, white painted wire and hardware. 
overall height 41in; width 9 1/4in; depth 5in

Cyndi Lauper has long regarded shoes as a site of artistic and personal expression, a practice that dates to her college years. For the celebrated photograph accompanying her 1983 album She's So Unusual, Lauper famously decorated a pair of shoes with imagery from Vincent van Gogh's "The Starry Night," now housed in the Smithsonian collection.

Lauper once reflected in an article by Leila Brillson for Refinery29: "...the soles of people's shoes...the fact that it's called the sole. Or the fact that sometimes, in your imagination, you could look through the bottom of the sole of your shoes, to see where that person was going or where they came from, or what they were thinking, or about their life."

The present work extends this longstanding meditation on shoes, movement, and the traces of human experience. A striking assemblage, it incorporates images of clouds photographed by Lauper herself, suspended in an arrangement that evokes a pair of shoes in motion, as though walking through an imagined landscape. The soles are inscribed with lyrics from the song "Time After Time," transforming the footwear into both visual and textual vessels. The words contemplate the paradoxes of intimacy and separation: the sensation of remaining emotionally connected even as two people move in different directions, evoking the bittersweet uncertainty inherent in all relationships:

"I'm walking to [sic] far ahead
you're calling to me I can't
hear what you say
Then you say go slow
I fall behind"

Here, Lauper's characteristic fusion of popular culture, personal symbolism, and visual invention gives material form to the experience of moving forward while remaining, in some sense, tethered to another. The shoes become metaphors for both departure and connection: objects that carry the imprint of where one has been while suggesting the unknowable path ahead.
